source_refs.note: Phase Lag and Phase Lead: a main subheading of 17.3 Phase of A.C., its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 90-91.

blocks.text: Referring to the Figs.17.5 (b) and 17.5(c), at t = 0, the angle θ is also 0°, the value of the phase angle θ at t equals to zero is called the initial phase of AC quantity. Thus, according to equations:

blocks.text_alt: V = Vₒ sin θ   and   I = Iₒ sin θ   (17.9)

blocks.text: which correspond to Figs.17.5(b) and 17.5(c) respectively, the initial phase of both voltage V and current I is zero. There are situations when current I and voltage V are not in phase i.e; they differ in phase. For example, the initial phase of current I may be positive or negative as compared to the initial phase of voltage V, which is zero. Consider a situation in which the initial phase of voltage V is zero and initial phase of current I is φ as shown in Fig.17.5 (b). This situation can be represented by the following equations:

blocks.text_alt: V = Vₒ sin θ   and   I = Iₒ sin (θ + φ)

blocks.text: At t = 0; voltage V = 0, but the current is positive and I = Iₒ sin φ. It means that the current had its zero value earlier by an angle φ than voltage. Thus, we can say that the current is leading the voltage by an angle φ in this situation (Fig. 17.5-b). The angle φ is the phase difference between the voltage and the current.

Similarly, the initial phase of current I is negative as compared to the initial phase of voltage V, which is zero as shown in Fig.17.5(c). This situation can be represented by the following equations:

blocks.text_alt: V = Vₒ sin θ   and   I = Iₒ sin (θ − φ)

blocks.text: It means the value of V is zero, but the current I has some negative value (I – sin φ). It means that the current I will reach its zero value later on by an angle φ than the voltage V. Thus, we can say that current I is lagging behind the voltage V by an angle φ. The angle φ is called the phase diffference between V and I.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the value at t = 0 as (I – sin φ); it is I = −Iₒ sin φ (put θ = 0 in I = Iₒ sin (θ − φ)). “diffference” is a misprint for difference.

blocks.alt: Two graphs against t. (b) Positive phase: the red current I = Io sin(theta + phi) starts a distance phi before t = 0, has the value Io sin phi at t = 0 and peaks at +Io before the green voltage V. (c) Negative phase: the current I = Io sin(theta - phi) has the value -Io sin phi at t = 0 and crosses zero phi after V.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.5 (b), (c): Graphical representation showing (b) current leads the voltage, (c) current lags behind voltage (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.5 (b), (c)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figures 17.5(b) and (c) give the values at t = 0 as 'Iₒ sin θ'. At t = 0 they are Iₒ sin φ and −Iₒ sin φ, as drawn above.
